paper_metadata.title: Strategies for multi-property optimization of solid-solution strengthened Ni-based superalloys through targeted precipitate engineering

evidence.quote: Solid-solution strengthened Ni-based superalloys are widely employed in high-temperature applications due to their excellent mechanical strength, creep resistance, and microstructural stability.

Representative alloys such as Inconel 617 and Haynes 230 achieve an optimized balance of strength, ductility, and corrosion resistance through multi-element solid-solution strengthening in conjunction with controlled precipitation hardening

These alloys typically adopt a face-centered cubic (FCC) γ matrix, where elements such as Cr, Fe, Al, Ti, Nb, and Mo are added to tune phase stability, lattice parameters, and interfacial behaviour

The γ ′ phase (Ni 3 (Al,Ti)) is the principal precipitation-strengthening phase in solid-solution strengthened Ni-based superalloys. It possesses an L1 2 -ordered structure, crystallizes in the face-centered cubic (FCC) system, and belongs to the Pm-3 m space group.
MC-type carbides (e.g., TiC, NbC) typically form during solidification and are generally observed as blocky or chain-like morphologies within grains or along grain boundaries.
In contrast, M 23 C 6 -type carbides primarily precipitate during aging or thermal exposure in the range of 600 – 1100 ◦ C.

The η phase (Ni 3 Ti) is a thermodynamically stable equilibrium phase that competes with the metastable γ ′ (Ni 3 (Al, Ti)) in Ni-based superalloys with high Ti/Al ratios. It crystallizes in the hexagonal D0 24 structure and typically precipitates under long-term aging or over-aging conditions

The σ phase is a representative TCP intermetallic compound characterized by high hardness and brittleness, which often leads to embrittlement and performance degradation, particularly under creep and thermal exposure conditions.
